summary: Between 28 September and 17 October 2023 an attacker used a service account credential to access Okta's customer support system and download files, including HAR files with session tokens. 134 customers had files accessed and 5 had sessions hijacked.

overview.background: Okta's support system holds customer support cases and attached files. HAR files record browser traffic and can contain session tokens.
systems: A service account with view and update permissions
An employee's Okta-managed laptop and personal Google account
overview.impact: 134 customers (less than 1 percent) had files accessed. The attacker used tokens to hijack sessions at 5 customers, and Cloudflare was the fifth.
overview.severity: Significant for a security vendor. Access lasted from 28 September to 17 October 2023.
overview.gaps: Okta says the likely exposure was a personal account or device compromise; it did not prove the exact path.

archNote: Components and relationships come from the cited source where it describes them. Layout and labels are ours.

diagrams.title: A saved credential opens the support system
diagrams.caption: Per Okta, the service account's username and password were saved in an employee's personal Google account via Chrome sign-in on an Okta-managed laptop.

nodes.label: Service account credential saved in personal profile
HAR files with session tokens downloaded

diagrams.title: Remediation Okta described (as a picture)
diagrams.caption: Block personal profiles, add detection and bind tokens to network location.

nodes.label: Personal Google profiles blocked in Chrome on managed laptops
Detection rules for the support system

afterChanges: Service credentials are not in personal profiles.
Stolen tokens are not usable elsewhere.
afterNote: The after picture shows the corrective ideas in the source and general good practice. It is conceptual unless the source says otherwise.
timelineNote: Times are as published by the source. Entries without a clock time are given in order only.

timeline.e: BeyondTrust provides a suspicious IP; Okta traces to the service account by 16 Oct.
Okta publishes root cause and remediation, and revokes tokens in the affected HAR files.

rootCause.trigger: An attacker obtained a service account credential saved in a personal Google account.
rootCause.underlying: The account could view and update customer support cases.
contributing: File downloads from the Files tab produced a different log event that was not flagged
A log gap hid the final hours
HAR files with live session tokens were attached to cases

evidence.label: The exposure path
evidence.body: The username and password of the service account had been saved into the employee's personal Google account.

evidence.label: Token risk
evidence.body: contained session tokens which could in turn be used for session hijacking attacks

diagnose.step: Check logs for all download paths.

verify.step: Check no further access from the actor.

prevent.step: Block personal profiles on managed devices.
Bind session tokens to network location.
Do not attach HAR files with live tokens.

fix.safety: Revoking tokens will sign users out. Communicate first.

troubleshoot.scenario: A customer reports suspicious sessions that trace back to a support case upload. Your logs show no downloads.
troubleshoot.question: What do you do?
hints: How do you find the access?
troubleshoot.answer: Search all download event types, disable the account, revoke tokens in exposed files, notify customers and fix logging.

rootcause.q: How many customers had files accessed?

remediation.answer: Alert on every file access path.

design.prompt: Design a support portal that avoids token leakage.
design.answer: Sanitisation on upload, scoped service accounts, complete logging and session binding.

checks.q: How many customers had sessions hijacked?
Who reported suspicious activity on 29 September?
What did Okta block on managed laptops?

sources.title: Okta: Unauthorized Access to Okta's Support Case Management System: Root Cause and Remediation

verification: Facts were read from Okta's report on 29 October 2026. Okta says the exposure path was likely, not proven, and this file keeps that wording.
